title: inference-trap-hypotheses-field-matrix
summary: A compact, workshop-friendly matrix that maps common buyer asks to competitor weak spots, probable trap lines, and quick rebuttals + demo checklist for Redwood Inference. Designed for AE/SE rapid prep and SDR sparring; focused on inference economics, reliability, and deployment flexibility.
content:
TL;DR:
Short checklist for the field: (1) surface buyer priority (latency/cost/security/SLAs); (2) map to competitor fault lines below; (3) use the 15–30s rebuttal + demo checklist; (4) escalate to Solutions Eng for Dedicated/Private questions.

How to use this doc:
- Quick read before calls (3–4 minutes).
- Use as a living artifact: add observed customer language to the trap column after each call.
- When a competitor name appears twice in the same call, flag for a post-call SE takeover.

Buyer ask -> Competitor weak spot -> Trap language (what they say) -> 15–30s Redwood counter -> Demo / Ask to qualify

1) "We care about predictable latency at scale"
- Common competitor weak spots: public multi-tenant endpoints with queueing spikes (variable p99), little control over batching or KV cache sharing; limited dedicated reservation options.
- Trap language: "We just need the best model and we'll accept occasional spikes." or "We can tune with retries on our side."
- 15–30s counter: "Predictable latency is an operational guarantee, not just a model choice. Redwood gives you reserved capacity and routing policies so your p50/p95/p99 don't move with noisy neighbors. We also expose batching and KV cache controls so you can trade throughput and cost without surprising tail latency."
- Demo/Qualify: Show per-route latency dashboard, 24h p99 trace, and the dedicated capacity config. Ask: "What does your acceptable p99 look like under peak traffic?"

2) "We're trying to minimize token spend / unit cost"
- Weak spots: vendors leaning on latest-gen large models only (no quantized variants), limited automatic prefix/KV cache, no smart batching controls, or unpredictable burst pricing.
- Trap language: "We'll just use smaller prompts or downscale model size when cost matters."
- 15–30s counter: "Cost is a system property — runtime, model quantization, cache, and routing. Redwood recommends quantized model variants and automated prefix caching plus workload-aware batching. That typically reduces per-token spend 3x–8x versus straight large-model calls while preserving output for most production prompts."
- Demo/Qualify: Show Optimize recommendations and a cost breakdown by token+model+batching. Ask: "What's your monthly token volume and current avg token cost?"

3) "We need full data isolation and KMS integration for HIPAA/PCI"
- Weak spots: hosted APIs that blur control plane vs data plane, limited KMS/HSM options, or no private control plane for audit logs.
- Trap language: "We can encrypt at rest in the vendor's cloud — that should be fine."
- 15–30s counter: "For regulated workloads the distinction between hosted convenience and auditable isolation matters. Redwood Private gives you a customer-controlled control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit log exports so your compliance team can attest to separation and key custody."
- Demo/Qualify: Walk through private deployment options, KMS integration flow, and sample audit log. Ask: "Do you need customer-managed keys or full air-gapped deployment?"

4) "How do you handle model regressions and quality drift?"
- Weak spots: vendors without eval/harness tooling or limited rollouts and no prompt-set-level regression alerts.
- Trap language: "We'll handle model validation in our QA after launch."
- 15–30s counter: "Redwood links quality monitoring to rollouts. You can register prompt sets and evaluation metrics, and get alerts tied to canary/A-B rollouts so regressions are caught before reaching production."
- Demo/Qualify: Show rollout UI and eval alerts; ask: "Do you have critical prompt families or business metrics to monitor?"

5) "We want a single API that works across cloud/on-prem"
- Weak spots: vendors with separate APIs or limited tooling for private deployments; inconsistent operational UX across hosted/dedicated/private.
- Trap language: "We prefer a single vendor — can you support our hybrid mix?"
- 15–30s counter: "Redwood's API is intentionally consistent across hosted, dedicated, and private — same SDK and rollout configs, same observability surface, and the same model catalog so you can migrate without rewriting client logic."
- Demo/Qualify: Show identical SDK snippet and authorization flow for hosted vs private. Ask: "What percentage of traffic must remain on-prem?"

Competitor-specific shorthand (field notes)
- OpenAI: Strength = model breadth + ecosystem. Weakness = black-box infra, limited reserved capacity controls, and policy changes can be abrupt. Field script: If they anchor on model quality-only, re-anchor to SLO and ops costs.
- Anthropic: Strength = safety-first model messaging. Weakness = cost/latency tradeoffs for strict model controls, limited private deployment options. Field script: Acknowledge safety leadership, pivot to deployment/ops controls.
- Google Vertex: Strength = integrations with cloud infra and data services. Weakness = vendor lock-in risk and inconsistent per-token economics across regions. Field script: Emphasize vendor independence and predictable economics.
- Cohere / Mistral / Smaller hosted models: Strength = price/experimental models. Weakness = variable SLOs and ecosystem support. Field script: Reinforce Redwood's routing and fallback to ensure availability.

Common field traps to listen for (and why they matter)
- "We'll just layer retries and caching on the client." (Why care: retried requests amplify spikes and hide root causes; caching at the client often duplicates work and lacks cross-instance warm cache).
- "We can custom-optimize the model on our side." (Why care: model changes are only one part — serving runtime, KV cache, batching and kernel selection also crucial and often overlooked.)
- "Price is the only metric." (Why care: lowest price without SLOs often leads to hidden costs: engineer time, retries, extra infra.)

Battle-tested 30s rebuttal templates (copy-friendly)
- Latency rebuttal: "If you prioritize consistent p99s, we should look at reserved capacity and routing policies — that’s where predictable user experience actually comes from, not just picking the latest model."
- Cost rebuttal: "We usually recommend measuring cost per coherent-response (includes retries and downstream processing) — Redwood's Optimize tools show that hitting your cost target often means small runtime tweaks, not big model downgrades."
- Security rebuttal: "We distinguish control plane from data plane; that difference often determines whether a SOC or compliance team approves a vendor."

Demo checklist (3–5 minute demo focused on objections)
- Pre-demo: load a sample prompt set that matches buyer use-case (customer support, summary, code).
- Show: per-route latency and cost breakdowns, a canary rollout from model-A -> model-B with eval metrics, dedicated capacity config, and a quick private deployment topology screenshot.
- Finish: show a cost delta projection from naive calls -> optimized (batching + cache + quantized model).

Escalation rules for AE/SE
- If buyer asks for formal SLA wording or interop with HSM/KMS: schedule SE + Security deep-dive (include infra and compliance SMEs).
- If buyer cites hard p99 requirement <150ms: flag for performance team to validate on target model and region.

Open questions to add to post-call notes (track as tags)
- Monthly token volume, burst patterns, peak concurrency targets, required p99, audit/KMS requirements, in-house model fine-tuning plans.

Appendix: quick tech counters (one-liners)
- Continuous batching: "Redwood supports continuous batching so we maximize GPU throughput without adding tail latency pressure."
- KV/prefix caching: "Prefix cache reduces repeated context cost and speeds up common flows (e.g., instruction-heavy prompts)."
- Quantized model variants: "We provide validated quantized variants so you get near-native quality with lower memory and cheaper inference."
- Smart routing & fallback: "Requests can be policy-routed by latency/cost/region and automatically fall back to compatible variants to avoid outage windows."

Notes to field: add real customer phrasing to the Trap column after every deal — this doc becomes more valuable with each iteration.

End.
